title: EUR 150,000 cover rejected, and the refund went to the wrong bank
explain:
A EUR 150,000 cover payment was rejected.
The bank holding the funds sent them back.
They went to the wrong bank, and one exception became two.

Here's how that happens:

→ Cover payment is rejected
→ Bank holding the cover returns the funds
→ Return sent to the wrong bank in the chain
→ Second exception opened on top of the first

The assumption was:
"Any bank in the chain can return the funds."
The funds must travel back along the same correspondent path they came on.

Why?

When a cover payment is rejected, the funds leg and the information leg have different senders, so the bank holding the rejected cover must return the funds to the bank that sent them. A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first.

A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first.

What proves the refund went back along the path the funds came on?

BA Takeaway

Return the funds to the bank that sent them, along the same correspondent path. Check the sender of the cover leg before returning, and treat a wrong-bank return as a new exception to be fixed, not a closed case.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bank that sent the cover
→ Correspondent path
→ Return received and matched

The real requirement isn't "Were the funds returned?"

It's "What evidence proves the refund went back along the path the funds came on?"

takeaway: A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first.

title: USD 85,000 return that tried to jump the chain
explain:
A USD 85,000 MT103 was returned.
The return was sent straight to the originator bank.
It never arrived, because the chain it had travelled on was skipped.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 is returned
→ Return sent directly to the originator
→ Intermediary banks skipped
→ Return cannot be matched, funds sit unreconciled

The assumption was:
"A return is a new payment, so send it direct."
A return is not a new payment.

Why?

When an MT103 is returned, the funds come back through the same chain of banks that carried the payment forward, each bank sending the return to the bank that sent it the payment. The charges on the return follow fields 71A and 71F, so the amount that comes back is the amount sent minus the charges already deducted.

A return is not a new payment. It is the original payment travelling backwards.

What proves the return travelled back through the same chain?

BA Takeaway

Send the return through the same banks that carried the payment forward, in reverse order. Apply fields 71A and 71F to the returned amount, and trace the return at every link.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return route
→ Fields 71A and 71F
→ Amount returned
→ Chain trace

The real requirement isn't "Was the return sent?"

It's "What evidence proves the return travelled back through the same chain?"

Have you ever chased a return that tried to jump the chain?
takeaway: A return is not a new payment. It is the original payment travelling backwards.

title: USD 40,000 sent to an account that did not exist
explain:
USD 40,000 was sent to a beneficiary account.
The account number was wrong.
The beneficiary bank could not credit anyone, and the customer asked where the money was.

Here's how that happens:

→ Beneficiary bank finds the account invalid
→ Wrong number, closed account or mismatched name
→ Beneficiary bank returns the payment
→ Return travels back through the intermediary to the originator

The assumption was:
"The beneficiary bank can sort it out and keep the funds."
The beneficiary bank cannot keep funds it cannot apply.

Why?

When the beneficiary bank finds the customer account invalid, it returns the payment, and the return must travel back through the intermediary to the originator bank. It cannot return the funds directly to the originator while an intermediary sits in between.

An invalid account is the most common reason for a return, and the handling never changes.

What proves the return is on its way back through the chain?

BA Takeaway

Return the payment through the intermediary, with the original references, and tell the customer the reason plainly. The handling is the same whether the fault is a wrong number, a closed account or a name that does not match.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason for the return
→ Return route through the intermediary
→ Original references
→ Customer told the reason

The real requirement isn't "Can the beneficiary bank keep the funds?"

It's "What evidence proves the return is on its way back through the chain?"

takeaway: An invalid account is the most common reason for a return, and the handling never changes.

title: EUR 60,000 settled, and the recall had nowhere to go
explain:
A customer asked for EUR 60,000 back after the payment had settled.
The originator bank sent a camt.056 recall.
The clearing house did not support the message, so the recall went nowhere.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment settles through the clearing house
→ Originator bank sends camt.056
→ Clearing house does not support the recall message
→ Recall cannot reach the beneficiary bank

The assumption was:
"Every clearing system carries recalls."
Some clearing houses do not support the camt.056 recall message.

Why?

The originator bank and the clearing system cannot send a recall to the beneficiary bank for a payment that has already settled when the clearing house does not support the message. The Estonian clearing house is a real example: it does not support the recall message, so a settled payment cannot be recalled through that route.

Know which clearing systems support a recall before promising a customer a payment can be taken back.

What proves this clearing system can carry a recall?

BA Takeaway

Check recall support before promising a customer a payment can be taken back. If the clearing house cannot carry a camt.056, say so early and find the route that can, instead of sending a recall into a dead end.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Clearing system
→ Recall support
→ Route that can carry the recall

The real requirement isn't "Can we recall this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves this clearing system can carry a recall?"

takeaway: Know which clearing systems support a recall before promising a customer a payment can be taken back.

title: EUR 110,000 recalled after the beneficiary had already spent it
explain:
EUR 110,000 was paid to the wrong beneficiary.
By the time the customer noticed, the beneficiary had already spent it.
The recall went out anyway, and the customer expected the money back.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment executed and funds spent
→ camt.056 sent to ask for the return
→ Beneficiary bank asks its customer whether it agrees
→ Funds no longer there, recall cannot complete by message alone

The assumption was:
"A recall reverses a payment."
Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

Why?

A camt.056 can still be sent to ask the beneficiary bank to return the money, but the beneficiary bank must ask its customer whether it agrees. If the funds are no longer there, the recall cannot be completed by message alone, and the customer must take action against the beneficiary.

Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

What proves the funds are still there to be returned?

BA Takeaway

Send the camt.056, but tell the customer plainly that the recall depends on the beneficiary agreeing and the funds still being there. If the money is gone, the recovery is a claim against the beneficiary, not a message.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Recall request sent
→ Beneficiary agreement
→ Funds still held
→ Recovery route if spent

The real requirement isn't "Can we reverse this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds are still there to be returned?"

Have you ever had to tell a customer a recall could not bring the money back?
takeaway: Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

title: EUR 70,000 recall for a third party, sent to the wrong bank
explain:
A EUR 70,000 recall was made in favour of a third-party beneficiary.
The recall was sent straight to the third party.
It sat unread, because the third party was never meant to receive it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Recall made for a third-party beneficiary
→ Recall sent directly to the third party
→ Third party cannot act on it
→ Recall stalls, funds stay put

The assumption was:
"The recall goes to the party the money is for."
The third party never receives the recall directly.

Why?

The recall is sent to the first agent in the chain, the bank that must return the credit, and that bank then passes the recall onward. The third party receives the result through the bank that acts for it.

The third party never receives the recall directly. It receives the result through the bank that acts for it.

What proves the recall reached the bank that must return the credit?

BA Takeaway

Send the recall to the first agent in the chain, not to the third party. Track the recall through the bank that acts for the third party, and report the result to the third party through that bank.

Keep these controls separate:

→ First agent in the chain
→ Bank that must return the credit
→ Result reported to the third party

The real requirement isn't "Who should receive this recall?"

It's "What evidence proves the recall reached the bank that must return the credit?"

title: EUR 55,000 recall rejected, with a reason code that did not belong there
explain:
A EUR 55,000 recall was refused.
The refusal came back as a pacs.004 carrying the reason code GVC.
GVC is not a code for a return, so the handling was wrong, and the case had to be reopened.

Here's how that happens:

→ camt.056 recall request sent
→ Recall refused
→ Refusal returned as pacs.004 with GVC
→ Code does not belong on a return, second exception opened

The assumption was:
"Any reason code explains a refusal."
A reason code must match the message and the situation.

Why?

A camt.056 recall request can itself be rejected, and the reason code on the refusal must fit the message carrying it. A pacs.004 carrying GVC is a code used in the wrong place, and it creates a second exception on top of the first.

A reason code must match the message and the situation.

What proves this reason code belongs on this message?

BA Takeaway

Check every reason code against the message it travels on and the situation it describes. Treat a mismatched code as a second exception, and correct it before the case can close.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code
→ Message it travels on
→ Situation it describes

The real requirement isn't "Does the code explain the refusal?"

It's "What evidence proves this reason code belongs on this message?"

Have you ever seen a refusal rejected again because of its own reason code?
takeaway: A reason code must match the message and the situation.

title: EUR 180,000 returned without a pacs.004, and the chain lost the link
explain:
EUR 180,000 had to come back.
The returning bank sent the funds by another route, not a pacs.004.
The money arrived, but no bank in the chain could prove which payment it belonged to.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment must be returned
→ Return sent by another route, not pacs.004
→ Funds arrive with no link to the original payment
→ Chain cannot match the return

The assumption was:
"Any route that moves the money is good enough."
Using another route breaks the link.

Why?

The pacs.004 is the ISO 20022 message designed for returns in the SEPA interbank space, and it carries the link to the original payment that lets every bank in the chain match it. Using another route breaks that link.

Using another route breaks the link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return.

What proves this return belongs to that original payment?

BA Takeaway

Return with a pacs.004, every time. Carry the original references on it, and treat a return that arrives by another route as unmatched until the link is proven some other way.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return message
→ Original references
→ Chain match

The real requirement isn't "Has the money come back?"

It's "What evidence proves this return belongs to that original payment?"

takeaway: Using another route breaks the link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return.

title: USD 95,000 serial recall that tried to skip a bank
explain:
A USD 95,000 serial MT103 had to be recalled.
The originator bank sent the recall straight to the beneficiary bank.
It failed, because the bank that was skipped still held the funds.

Here's how that happens:

→ Originator bank sends the recall
→ Recall skips the intermediary banks
→ Skipped bank still holds the funds
→ Recall fails, money stays put

The assumption was:
"The recall only needs the two ends."
A serial MT103 can be recalled, but the recall must travel the same chain.

Why?

The originator bank sends the recall to the next bank in the chain, and each bank passes it on until it reaches the beneficiary bank, which decides whether the funds can be returned. A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds.

A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds.

What proves the recall travelled the same chain as the payment?

BA Takeaway

Send the recall bank by bank, along the chain the payment took. Track it at every link, and let the beneficiary bank decide on the funds only after the recall has reached it through the chain.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Recall route
→ Each bank in the chain
→ Beneficiary bank decision
→ Funds returned

The real requirement isn't "Was the recall sent to the beneficiary bank?"

It's "What evidence proves the recall travelled the same chain as the payment?"

takeaway: A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds.

title: EUR 200,000 cover arrived EUR 150 short
explain:
An MT103 announced EUR 200,000.
The cover arrived for EUR 199,850.
An intermediary had taken its EUR 150 charge from the cover, and the beneficiary bank refused to credit the short amount.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 announces EUR 200,000
→ Intermediary takes EUR 150 from the MT202 COV
→ Cover arrives EUR 150 short
→ Beneficiary bank holds the payment

The assumption was:
"An intermediary can take its charge from the cover."
It is forbidden to take charges from an MT202 COV.

Why?

The cover amount must never be lower than the amount announced in the MT103. If an intermediary needs to be paid for its part in the chain, it asks the sending bank to pay through an MT191 or debits the account directly under the agreement between the banks.

A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is an exception, not a normal deduction.

What proves the cover matches the announced amount in full?

BA Takeaway

Never deduct from a cover. Claim charges separately through an MT191 or by direct debit under the agreement, and treat any short cover as an exception to be fixed before crediting.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Amount announced
→ Cover amount
→ Charges claimed separately
→ Exception on a short cover

The real requirement isn't "Is the cover a little short?"

It's "What evidence proves the cover matches the announced amount in full?"

Have you ever had a cover arrive short because a charge was taken from it?
takeaway: A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is an exception, not a normal deduction.

title: USD 45,000 missing for two weeks, and everyone said to wait
explain:
USD 45,000 was sent to a supplier.
Three days passed. Then a week. Then two.
Everyone said to wait a little longer, while the supplier threatened to stop deliveries.

Here's how that happens:

→ Transfer sent in a major currency
→ 48 to 72 hours pass, nothing arrives
→ One week passes, still nothing
→ Two weeks pass, still nothing

The assumption was:
"Cross-border payments just take a while."
After two weeks, there is definitely a problem.

Why?

A transfer in a major currency such as the United States dollar or the euro usually arrives in 48 to 72 hours, while a transfer in a less common local currency takes longer because the currency is harder to buy. A large amount can also slow a payment down, because it may need extra checks before it is released.

If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem.

What proves this payment is still moving, rather than lost?

BA Takeaway

Ask the sending bank to trace it. The sending bank knows every party in the chain, and a trace, not more waiting, is what finds a payment that has not arrived after two weeks.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Time since sending
→ Currency and amount checks
→ Trace requested
→ Every party in the chain named

The real requirement isn't "Should we keep waiting?"

It's "What evidence proves this payment is still moving, rather than lost?"

Have you ever waited two weeks for a payment everyone said was just slow?
takeaway: If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem.

title: EUR 70,000 MT103 with an IBAN but no name
explain:
An MT103 for EUR 70,000 arrived showing only the beneficiary's IBAN and address in field 59.
No name at all.
The beneficiary bank held the payment, unable to confirm the account belonged to the person the payment was meant for.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 shows only IBAN and address in field 59
→ No beneficiary name
→ Bank cannot confirm the account owner
→ Bank holds the payment and asks for confirmation

The assumption was:
"An IBAN identifies the beneficiary."
Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary.

Why?

Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary, so a missing name leaves the beneficiary bank unable to confirm that the account belongs to the person the payment was meant for. The bank may hold the payment and ask for confirmation instead of crediting it, and the sender's bank is the one that must supply the missing name.

A missing name leaves the bank unable to confirm the account belongs to the right person.

What proves the account belongs to the person this payment was meant for?

BA Takeaway

Supply the beneficiary name in field 59 on every MT103. When a payment arrives without one, hold it, ask the sender's bank for the name, and credit only when the name and the account agree.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Beneficiary name in field 59
→ IBAN and address
→ Name and account agree
→ Credit only on agreement

The real requirement isn't "Is the IBAN enough?"

It's "What evidence proves the account belongs to the person this payment was meant for?"

title: EUR 12,000 SDD collection, silence for a week, and the team assumed it had failed
explain:
A EUR 12,000 direct debit collection went out as a pacs.007.
A week passed in silence.
The team assumed the collection had failed and sent it again, and the debtor was debited twice.

Here's how that happens:

→ Creditor bank sends pacs.007
→ No scheme response follows
→ Team reads silence as failure
→ Collection sent again, debtor debited twice

The assumption was:
"Silence means it failed."
Silence after pacs.007 is normal, not failure.

Why?

Under the SDD scheme the debtor bank sends no scheme response once it has the pacs.007 collection instruction, so silence after that point says nothing about the outcome. When the collection comes back, it arrives as a pacs.004 return or refund, and the creditor bank must process it without any option to refuse.

Silence after pacs.007 is normal, not failure.

What proves this collection failed, rather than simply being silent?

BA Takeaway

Wait for the outcome instead of resending. Build processing around handling pacs.004 returns and refunds, which the creditor bank must process without any option to refuse, and never treat silence as a failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.007 sent
→ Silence expected
→ pacs.004 return handled
→ No resend on silence

The real requirement isn't "Has the collection failed?"

It's "What evidence proves this collection failed, rather than simply being silent?"

Have you ever resent a collection because silence looked like failure?

title: A pacs.004 arrived for EUR 50,000. Return or refund? Nobody could tell.
explain:
A pacs.004 for EUR 50,000 lands in the queue.
The customer is waiting for an answer.
The team cannot tell whether it is a return or a refund.

Here is how that happens:

→ pacs.004 received for EUR 50,000
→ Initiator field checked
→ Return rules and refund rules both look possible
→ Payment held while the team argues

The requirement said:
"A pacs.004 is a return."

Why?

A pacs.004 can carry either a return or a refund. The debtor bank starts a return, the debtor starts a refund, and the two events run under different rules and different time limits. Reading the message type alone tells you nothing. Only the initiator tells you which event it is.

One message, two events. Read the initiator.

BA Takeaway

Treat the initiator as the first check on every pacs.004, before any rule or time limit is applied.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return status
→ Refund status
→ Initiator identity

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves whether this pacs.004 is a return or a refund?"

Have you ever held a payment because the message type alone could not tell you what it was?

title: EUR 1,200 collected with no mandate. The debtor claims it back, 12 months later.
explain:
A EUR 1,200 direct debit was collected every month.
Twelve months later the debtor says there was never a valid mandate.
The creditor is sure the 8 week refund window has closed.

Here is how that happens:

→ SDD Core collection of EUR 1,200
→ Debtor claims a refund after 12 months
→ Creditor checks the 8 week window
→ Mandate checked and found missing

The requirement said:
"Refunds are always claimed within 8 weeks."

Why?

In SDD Core the 8 week window applies only where a valid mandate stands behind the collection. Where no valid mandate exists at all, the window is 13 months. The two periods must never be confused, and the creditor holds the mandate, so the creditor must produce it when a claim is disputed.

8 weeks needs a mandate. No mandate means 13 months.

BA Takeaway

Record which window applies on every refund claim, and ask for the mandate before arguing about the date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate validity
→ Refund window
→ Mandate evidence

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves a valid mandate existed for this collection?"

Have you seen a refund claim turn on a mandate nobody could produce?
takeaway: 8 weeks needs a mandate. No mandate means 13 months.

title: EUR 200,000 to a new corridor. The intermediary could not serve it, and the payment died.
explain:
A EUR 200,000 payment is sent down a new corridor.
The instruction names an intermediary that holds no settlement relationship there.
The payment dies downstream, and message mapping, routing data and routing logic all look equally guilty.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 200,000 sent on a new corridor
→ Intermediary named in the instruction
→ Intermediary cannot serve the destination currency
→ Payment rejected downstream

The requirement said:
"If the payment fails downstream, the mapping must be wrong."

Why?

An instruction can name an intermediary that cannot serve the destination currency and holds no settlement relationship for that corridor, and the payment dies downstream. The failure is then unreadable: message mapping, routing reference data and routing logic all look equally guilty. Start from the agent chain data, validate every intermediary against the corridor, repair the reference data, and track repair rates so the bad intermediary is caught before its next payment.

Start from the agent chain, not from the mapping.

BA Takeaway

Validate every intermediary against its corridor before the payment goes out, and track repair rates so bad data is caught early.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Agent chain data
→ Intermediary corridor coverage
→ Reference data repair

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this intermediary serves this corridor and currency?"

Have you chased a mapping fault that turned out to be bad intermediary data?
takeaway: Start from the agent chain, not from the mapping.

title: EUR 80,000 held at the border. The purpose code was optional at the front, mandatory at the back.
explain:
A customer sends EUR 80,000 abroad and leaves the purpose code blank, because the screen says it is optional.
Downstream, a system that mandates the code holds the payment.
Nobody owns the repair, so the payment waits while the customer calls.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 80,000 payment sent without a purpose code
→ Code optional at the customer, mandatory downstream
→ Payment held at the downstream system
→ No named owner for the repair

The requirement said:
"An optional field can stay optional all the way through."

Why?

A purpose code that is optional at the customer and mandatory downstream is a defect waiting for a payment. Name the downstream system that needs it, give enrichment a named owning source, and validate early enough to catch a missing code before the payment reaches that system. And define the repair behaviour up front, who fixes it, how fast, and what happens to the payment while it waits.

Optional at the front, mandatory at the back, is a defect.

BA Takeaway

Name the downstream system, the enrichment owner and the repair behaviour for every code that is mandatory anywhere in the chain.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Downstream requirement
→ Enrichment owner
→ Repair behaviour

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payment carries every code the downstream system needs?"

Have you watched a payment stall on a field the customer was told was optional?
takeaway: Optional at the front, mandatory at the back, is a defect.

title: EUR 120,000 routed to a bank that stopped serving the corridor years ago.
explain:
A EUR 120,000 payment is routed through an intermediary named in the reference data.
The bank stopped serving that corridor years ago, and nobody updated the data.
The payment is rejected, and the same bad intermediary is used again next week.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 120,000 routed via Intermediary Agent 2
→ Reference data points at a bank that left the corridor
→ Payment rejected downstream
→ Same intermediary used again the next week

The requirement said:
"Reference data looks after itself."

Why?

Reference data without an owner decays, and Intermediary Agent 2 is the proof: nobody maintains it, so it quietly points payments at a bank that no longer serves the corridor. The control set is fourfold, a named owner, a validation rule, an update process, and a routing control that stops a payment whose intermediary data is out of date. Leave any of the four out and the same bad intermediary keeps reappearing until a rejection or a repair exposes it.

Reference data without an owner decays.

BA Takeaway

Give every intermediary field a named owner, a validation rule, an update process and a routing block on stale data.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Named owner
→ Validation rule
→ Update process
→ Routing block

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this intermediary data is current today?"

Have you seen the same bad intermediary reappear after a rejection?
takeaway: Reference data without an owner decays.

title: EUR 25,000 collected from a customer who cancelled. The file was built on last month's data.
explain:
A collection file goes out for EUR 25,000.
It includes a customer who cancelled, and an amount changed after the file was built.
The file is submitted after the scheme deadline, and the refunds and complaints arrive together.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection file built on old data
→ Cancelled customer still collected
→ Amount changed after the file was built
→ File submitted after the scheme deadline

The requirement said:
"A collection file is a spreadsheet job."

Why?

Treat a collection file as a regulated scheme submission, not a spreadsheet job: the same errors return every month, a cancelled customer still collected, an amount changed after the file was built, a file submitted after the scheme deadline. The discipline is the sequence, build from current mandate and billing data, validate, win creditor PSP acceptance, submit inside the scheme window. Skip a step and the cost arrives as refunds, complaints and rework.

A collection file is a scheme submission, not a spreadsheet job.

BA Takeaway

Run the file through the full sequence every time, and never submit a file built on stale data.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Current mandate data
→ File validation
→ Creditor PSP acceptance
→ Scheme window

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this file was built on current data and submitted inside the window?"

Have you seen the same collection errors return every month?
takeaway: A collection file is a scheme submission, not a spreadsheet job.

title: A customer cancelled a EUR 800 collection. The money was still debited.
explain:
A customer asks billing to cancel a EUR 800 collection.
Billing deletes it from the file.
The file is already with the creditor PSP, so the debit goes ahead anyway.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 800 collection submitted to the creditor PSP
→ Customer asks for cancellation
→ Billing deletes it from the local file
→ Collection debited because deletion no longer works

The requirement said:
"Deleting it from the file cancels the collection."

Why?

Once a file is with the creditor PSP, cancelling a collection is a scheme process, not a delete key. Cancellation follows the process for the collection state at that moment, and a collection already in processing can only be stopped on the defined cancellation path. Billing must know the exact lifecycle point where deletion stops working and cancellation takes over, because that point decides whether the customer is debited.

After submission, deletion stops working. Cancellation takes over.

BA Takeaway

Teach billing the exact lifecycle point where deletion ends and the scheme cancellation path begins.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Collection lifecycle state
→ Deletion window
→ Scheme cancellation path

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this collection was cancelled on the right path for its state?"

Have you deleted a collection that was already with the PSP?
takeaway: After submission, deletion stops working. Cancellation takes over.

title: A member cancelled. A clerk revoked. The EUR 300 collection was debited anyway.
explain:
A member cancels a membership and expects no further collection.
A billing clerk revokes the next EUR 300 collection instead.
The wrong mechanism is used for the collection's state, and the member is debited anyway.

Here is how that happens:

→ Member cancels the membership
→ Clerk revokes the EUR 300 collection
→ Wrong mechanism for the collection state
→ Member debited despite the cancellation

The requirement said:
"Cancellation and revocation are the same thing."

Why?

Cancellation and revocation are different mechanisms that happen to sound alike: different parties start them, at different times, for collections in different states. A member cancelling a membership expects no further collection, a billing clerk revoking a collection expects it never to leave the building, and a creditor PSP receiving a cancellation request expects a scheme message with a response. Choose by collection state, because the wrong mechanism debits the member anyway or gets the request rejected by the bank.

Same word, different mechanism. State picks it.

BA Takeaway

Choose the mechanism by collection state, and name the state on every cancellation and revocation request.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Collection state
→ Cancelling path
→ Revoking path

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this collection was in the state this mechanism serves?"

title: A duplicate EUR 1,100 collection settled. Someone deleted it, and reconciliation broke.
explain:
A duplicate EUR 1,100 collection settles by mistake.
Someone deletes the settled entry to fix it.
Reconciliation now has a hole where the money went, and the audit trail is gone.

Here is how that happens:

→ Duplicate EUR 1,100 collection settles
→ Entry deleted to fix the duplicate
→ Reconciliation finds a hole
→ Audit trail lost

The requirement said:
"A settled duplicate can be deleted to fix it."

Why?

A reversal is its own transaction, not a deletion and not a debtor refund claim: a separate, linked entry returning money already settled, used when a duplicate collection can no longer be cancelled or revoked because the money has moved. It carries the original references, is initiated by the creditor, and posts as its own accounting entry so reconciliation pairs it with the original instead of finding a hole. Deleting settled entries breaks reconciliation, so the duplicate is reversed, never erased.

Settled money is reversed, never erased.

BA Takeaway

Reverse a settled duplicate as its own linked transaction, with the original references attached.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Original collection
→ Reversal entry
→ Reconciliation pair

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this duplicate was reversed, not deleted?"

title: A pacs.008 for EUR 60,000 was rejected. The team sent a pacs.004 to fix it.
explain:
A pacs.008 for EUR 60,000 is rejected before settlement.
The pacs.002 carries status RJCT and a reason code.
The team opens a return, even though no money has moved.

Here is how that happens:

→ pacs.008 for EUR 60,000 sent
→ pacs.002 returns RJCT with a reason code
→ Team opens a pacs.004 return
→ No money has moved, so there is nothing to return

The requirement said:
"A rejected payment is fixed with a return."

Why?

An RJCT on a pacs.002 is a pre-settlement verdict: the status report says the instruction failed, and no money has moved. The reason code names the failure precisely, technical, such as a schema or format error, or business, such as a sanctions flag, and each kind has its own owner. The remedy is repair at source and resubmission as a new instruction, new message ID, same UETR, so tracking stays continuous.

RJCT before settlement means repair, not return.

BA Takeaway

Classify the RJCT by reason code, repair at source, and resubmit on the same UETR.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.002 RJCT status
→ Reason code
→ Resubmission on the same UETR

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves no money moved, so repair is the right remedy?"

takeaway: RJCT before settlement means repair, not return.

A EUR 90,000 payment settles, then turns out to be wrong.
The team sends another pacs.002 to fix it.
Nothing moves, because a status report never moves money.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 90,000 payment settles
→ Error found after settlement
→ Team tries a pacs.002 to fix it
→ Funds stay where they are

The requirement said:
"A status report can fix a settled payment."

Why?

Settlement closes the pacs.002 path for good: a status report never moves money, so a settled payment cannot be fixed by reporting. The funds must come back through a pacs.004, a real settlement instruction in reverse, travelling the return chain through every bank the original passed. Return charges may come off along the way, so the amount returning can differ from the amount sent, and the UETR ties both legs together for reconciliation.

After settlement, only a return moves money.

BA Takeaway

Once a payment is settled, open a pacs.004 and trace the return chain, never another status report.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Settlement state
→ pacs.004 return
→ UETR linkage

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payment settled, so only a return can move it?"

title: EUR 40,000 credited to a closed account. The beneficiary bank sent it back itself.
explain:
EUR 40,000 is credited to an account, then found to be closed.
The beneficiary bank does not wait to be asked.
It sends the money back itself, and the sender waits for a recall that never comes.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 40,000 credited
→ Account found closed after the credit
→ Beneficiary bank opens a pacs.004
→ Sender waits for a recall request

The requirement said:
"Only the sender can start a return."

Why?

A beneficiary bank that credits an account and then finds it closed or frozen does not wait to be asked. It becomes the return originator and sends the pacs.004 back along the chain in reverse. Charges may be deducted at hops, so the sender recovers the original minus charges, and the return is matched to the original payment by UETR.

The beneficiary bank can send the money back itself.

BA Takeaway

When funds land on a closed or frozen account, expect the beneficiary bank to originate the return, and match it by UETR.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Closed account finding
→ Beneficiary bank return
→ UETR match

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves who originated this return?"

title: A EUR 110,000 payment timed out. The team retried it blind, and paid twice.
explain:
A EUR 110,000 payment times out mid-chain.
Nobody knows whether it settled.
The team retries it, and the beneficiary is paid twice.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 110,000 payment times out
→ Outcome unknown, no status received
→ Blind retry sent
→ Beneficiary paid twice

The requirement said:
"A timeout means the payment failed, so retry it."

Why?

A timeout reports nothing about the outcome, and a blind retry on an unknown can double-pay. Freeze the payment, then work the evidence, UETR, EndToEndId and TxId across the tracker and hop logs, late responses, and statements against camt.054 notifications. Act only on the true state found: resubmit if it truly failed, recall or claim if it settled incorrectly.

A timeout is an unknown, not a failure.

BA Takeaway

Freeze every timed-out payment, prove its true state from the tracker and the statements, and act only on what you find.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Timeout state
→ UETR evidence
→ Statement proof

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves whether this payment settled or failed?"

takeaway: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure.

lesson.label: Chapter 51: Payment Reconciliation

agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 110,000 payment timed out. The team retried it blind, and paid twice.. A EUR 110,000 payment times out mid-chain. Nobody knows whether it settled. The team retries it, and the beneficiary is paid twice. One thing to remember: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure.

title: USD 75,000 from India to the USA vanished between hops. The tracker showed the last good hop.
explain:
A USD 75,000 payment leaves India for the USA.
It never reaches the beneficiary.
The team searches the whole chain at once, and finds nothing.

Here is how that happens:

→ USD 75,000 pacs.008 sent from India
→ Fedwire leg never completes
→ Team searches the whole chain
→ Failure point never found

The requirement said:
"A failed cross-border payment is investigated as one rail."

Why?

Cross-border tracing works leg by leg, never as one rail: a SWIFT pacs.008 moves across correspondents, then Fedwire completes final US dollar settlement. Start from the UETR in the tracker, locate the last successful hop, and read the status message there, because its reason code names the failure. Then test the corridor suspects, a missing purpose code, a sanctions hold, an invalid routing number, or an FX or cut-off gap, and close the case with the right message, a pacs.004 return or a camt.056 recall.

Trace leg by leg, from the last good hop.

BA Takeaway

Start every cross-border trace at the UETR, find the last good hop, and test the corridor suspects in order.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR tracker
→ Last good hop
→ Reason code

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves where this payment stopped?"

Have you searched a whole chain when the last good hop would have told you?
takeaway: Trace leg by leg, from the last good hop.

title: A EUR 95,000 payment timed out mid-chain. The recall was the brake, and it was pulled too late.
explain:
A EUR 95,000 payment times out mid-chain with its state unknown.
The team debates whether to recall it.
By the time the recall goes out, the credit has completed, and the recall cannot undo it.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 95,000 pacs.008 times out
→ True state unknown
→ Recall debated instead of sent
→ Credit completes before the recall lands

The requirement said:
"A recall can undo a completed payment."

Why?

A payment timed out mid-chain with its true state unknown is exactly when a recall earns its name as an emergency brake: send the request down the chain and stop it before it completes. The brake has one limit, it cannot undo a completed credit. Where the credit already completed, switch to the return flow via pacs.004, and update the customer at each step, because silence turns incidents into escalations.

A recall is a brake, not a reverse gear.

BA Takeaway

Pull the recall the moment a payment times out mid-chain, and switch to a pacs.004 the moment the credit completes.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Timeout point
→ Recall request
→ Return flow

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payment is still stoppable, not already credited?"

Have you pulled the recall brake too late?
takeaway: A recall is a brake, not a reverse gear.
